outcome: No proof, disproof, or substantive new progress on the infinitude of Pell primes was found since 26 January 2024; the conjecture remains open and is believed to follow from Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture F, which is itself unresolved.
summary: Are there infinitely many Pell primes? remains open. Pell primes are Pell numbers P(n) = ((1+√2)^n − (1−√2)^n)/(2√2) that are themselves prime; as with Fibonacci primes, a necessary (not sufficient) condition is that the index n be prime. The conjecture that infinitely many exist is understood to be a consequence of Hardy–Littlewood's Conjecture F (on primes represented by binary quadratic/other low-degree forms related to the Pell recurrence), which is itself a decades-old open conjecture with no proof in the window. I checked: (1) the Wikipedia articles for Pell number and List of unsolved problems in mathematics, neither of which record any change; (2) OEIS A096650 (indices n for which P(n) is prime or probable prime), whose data (31 known indices, largest 90197) and comments were last substantively added to well before 2024 — the only 2025-era addition is an unrelated citing reference (Fan & Pollack, 'Extremal elasticity of quadratic orders', arXiv:2503.07801) that merely references the sequence in passing, not a result about the conjecture; (3) secondary summaries (Googology Wiki, MathWorld-derived search snippets) confirming the largest *proven* Pell prime (index 13339) dates to 2001 and the largest known *probable* Pell prime (index 90197) dates to 2004 — both well before the window, and in any case a new large (probable) prime would not bear on the infinitude question per the scope rules in §3.1, since finding one more term does not answer an existence question; (4) targeted arXiv/web searches for any 2024–2026 proof, disproof or conjecture-strength progress specific to Pell primes, which turned up nothing on point — the only 2024–2025 papers found involving 'Pell' and primality concern unrelated topics: a primality *test* built on the geometry of Pell's cubic (arXiv:2411.01638), pseudoprimality via the Pell conic (arXiv:2001.00353, pre-window), and general AI-for-number-theory surveys that do not mention Pell primes. None of these change what could be written in this Wikipedia bullet. I found no AI involvement of any kind in connection with this specific conjecture.
competing_reading: One could argue that continued discovery/verification of larger probable Pell primes (the OEIS list, last extended pre-2024) constitutes 'progress' worth a `progress` status even though it doesn't touch the infinitude question, since it narrows nothing about the underlying existence claim. I judged this not to count, consistent with §3.1's rule that record extensions for an existence/infinitude question don't count unless the record IS the question (which it is not here — the question is about infinitude, not about the largest known example) — and in any case no such extension occurred inside the window.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture F (or a direct, unconditional proof/disproof of infinitely many Pell primes bypassing it) would settle this. Short of that, only a further-reaching heuristic/analytic result specifically about Pell primes (not merely citing the sequence) would count as `progress`.
